# **ABSTRACT** {#abstract}

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems enable users to query private document collections using natural language without retraining large language models, making them well-suited for domain-specific applications such as legal question answering. However, limited empirical guidance exists on key RAG design choices, including chunking strategy, chunk size, and generator model selection. This project investigates these factors through a controlled experimental study using Terms of Service documents, which contain complex legal language, structured clauses, and require high response accuracy. In the first phase, five chunking strategies: fixed-size, recursive character, sentence-based, semantic, and section-aware are evaluated across three chunk sizes (256, 512, and 1024 tokens). Performance is measured using a 30-question ground-truth dataset and assessed on retrieval quality, faithfulness, correctness, latency, and token cost, with non-parametric statistical tests and bootstrap confidence intervals used to compare configurations. The second phase compares a paid model, Claude Opus 4.8, with the open-source Llama-3.1-8B model using the best-performing chunking configuration. The study aims to provide practical, evidence-based recommendations for optimizing RAG systems in legal document retrieval and question-answering tasks.

**Keywords: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, RAG pipeline, chunking strategy, chunk size, legal document QA, Terms of Service, Large Language Models, faithfulness, Llama, Claude, vector search, Cloudflare Worker**

# **CHAPTER 1**   {#chapter-1}

# **INTRODUCTION**  {#introduction}

## **1.1 Background**  {#1.1-background}

Artificial Intelligence systems capable of answering natural language questions over private document collections have become increasingly relevant across industries. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is one such architecture, combining a document retrieval mechanism with a Large Language Model (LLM) to produce grounded, context-aware responses (Lewis et al., 2020). Unlike model fine-tuning, RAG requires no retraining and can be applied to any document corpus, making it practical for domain-specific use cases.  
Terms of Service and Terms and Conditions agreements represent a particularly important application domain. These documents are dense with legal terminology and structured across many clauses, yet users frequently need to extract specific information from them, such as account termination conditions, refund policies, data usage rights, and liability limitations. Manual review of such documents is time-consuming and error-prone, and most users do not read them in full. A well-configured RAG system could enable accurate, grounded natural language querying of these documents.  
Despite growing adoption of RAG, research indicates that pipeline performance is highly sensitive to configuration choices particularly how documents are segmented before indexing (chunking strategy), how large each segment is (chunk size), and which generator model produces the final answer. These three configuration variables jointly determine whether a deployed system gives faithful, fast, and cost-effective answers.  
There is limited empirical guidance for structured legal documents, where section-based organisation and clause-heavy language differ substantially from general text. This project addresses that gap by conducting a controlled empirical study of chunking strategy, chunk size, and generator model choice on a corpus of two real Terms of Service documents from two different organisations, using a purpose-built evaluation pipeline with custom retrieval-quality, faithfulness, correctness, latency, and token-cost metrics.

## **1.2 Problem Statement** {#1.2-problem-statement}

A developer building a Retrieval-Augmented Generation system over legal documents today must make three configuration choices with no domain-specific empirical evidence to guide them: which chunking strategy to use, what chunk size to set, and which generator model to deploy, so that performance can be optimized. The wrong combination can produce confident but wrong answers about cancellation terms, refund policies, or data-usage clauses, exactly the questions users most need correct answers to. As a result, practitioners must rely on intuition or general-purpose defaults, with no published evidence on:

- which chunking strategy best preserves the semantic structure of documents  
- what chunk size produces the highest retrieval precision and answer quality  
- whether a paid generator model offers materially better answer quality, latency, or cost than a freely available open-source model when the rest of the pipeline is held constant.

RAG system performance on Terms of Service documents is poorly understood in the context of three configuration choices that every practitioner must make.

## **1.3 Objectives** {#1.3-objectives}

Our project aims:

- To study the effect of chunking strategy and chunk size on answer quality   
- To compare a paid and an open-source generator model on answer quality, latency, and token cost, under the identified optimal chunking configuration.

## **1.4 Implications** {#1.4-implications}

The findings of this study will provide:

1. Practical, evidence-based guidance for developers configuring RAG pipelines for Terms of Service question answering by producing a direct comparison that practitioners can consult when choosing a chunking strategy, chunk size, and generator model for a structured legal document.  
2. A foundation for future work on RAG configuration for legal documents. Because the three variables are studied while other configuration choices (embedding model, retrieval depth, prompt template, hybrid retrieval) are held constant, the analysis provides a clean baseline that future studies can extend by varying those other variables.

# **CHAPTER 2** {#chapter-2}

# **LITERATURE REVIEW** {#literature-review}

## **2.1 Similar Literatures** {#2.1-similar-literatures}

### **2.1.1 Chunk Twice, Embed Once: A Systematic Study of Segmentation and Representation Trade-offs in Chemistry-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation**

Amiri and Bocklitz (2025) present the first large-scale study jointly evaluating chunking strategies and embedding models for domain-specific RAG, testing 25 chunking configurations and 48 embedding models across three chemistry-focused retrieval benchmarks. The central finding is that recursive token-based chunking without overlap (RT100-0) consistently outperforms all other strategies, achieving 45% higher precision than the best fixed-size alternative, while increasing overlap beyond 20% reduces precision significantly without improving recall. The study also demonstrates that chunking configuration has as much impact on retrieval quality as embedding model selection, making both equally important design decisions in any RAG pipeline (Amiri & Bocklitz, 2025).

### **2.1.2 A Systematic Analysis of Chunking Strategies for Reliable Question Answering** 

Bennani and Moslonka (2025) systematically study how chunking decisions affect RAG reliability in industrial settings, testing four chunking methods—token, sentence, semantic, and code-based, across different chunk sizes, overlap ratios, and context lengths using SPLADE retrieval and Mistral-8B on the Natural Questions benchmark. The study finds that adding chunk overlap provides no measurable quality improvement while increasing indexing cost, and that sentence chunking performs as well as the more expensive semantic chunking up to 5,000 context tokens. A notable finding is the context cliff effect, where quality drops beyond approximately 2,500 tokens because the model becomes distracted by irrelevant retrieved content rather than benefiting from additional context. The study also shows that the optimal context length depends on the evaluation goal, with smaller contexts favouring semantic quality and larger contexts favouring exact factual accuracy (Bennani & Moslonka, 2025).

### **2.1.3 CRAG \- Comprehensive RAG Benchmark**

Yang et al. (2024) introduce CRAG, a large-scale benchmark developed at Meta AI Research to evaluate how accurately RAG systems answer questions without hallucinating. The benchmark contains 4,409 questions across five domains, categorised by how frequently facts change, how popular the entities are, and how complex the question is, with responses scored as correct, incomplete, or hallucinated. The key finding is that even the best RAG systems answer only 63% of questions correctly without hallucination, performing worse on rapidly changing facts, obscure entities, and questions that require combining information from multiple sources. The study also shows that improving retrieval alone is not enough, as the language model itself independently introduces errors during generation, meaning both retrieval and generation stages must be evaluated and improved separately  (Yang et al., 2024).

### **2.1.4. Seven Failure Points When Engineering a Retrieval Augmented Generation System** 

Barnett et al. (2024) identify and analyse seven recurring failure points in production RAG systems based on practical engineering experience, providing one of the few practitioner-oriented diagnoses of where RAG pipelines break down in real deployments. The most critical finding is that document chunking is a primary failure point, as fixed-size chunking frequently splits semantically coherent units such as paragraphs, tables, and structured sections, causing the retriever to return incomplete or contextually broken passages that degrade generation quality regardless of how capable the language model is. Other identified failure points include missed retrieval due to vocabulary mismatch, context window overflow from retrieving too many chunks, incorrect answer extraction when the relevant content is present but not properly surfaced, and hallucination introduced when retrieved context is ambiguous or contradictory. The paper concludes that robust RAG engineering requires structure-aware chunking strategies, careful calibration of the number of retrieved chunks, and post-retrieval validation steps, directly motivating the inclusion of recursive and section-aware chunking as experimental strategies in any systematic RAG evaluation (Barnett et al., 2024).

### **2.1.5 Towards Reliable Retrieval in RAG Systems for Large Legal Datasets**

*Towards Reliable Retrieval in RAG Systems for Large Legal Datasets*  address a specific failure mode in RAG systems when applied to large legal document corpora. The paper identifies that RAG's reliability is critically dependent on the accuracy of the retrieval step, which is particularly challenging in the legal domain where large databases of structurally similar documents often cause retrieval systems to fail. To address this, the authors identify and quantify a failure mode termed Document-Level Retrieval Mismatch (DRM), where the retriever selects information from entirely incorrect source documents, and propose Summary-Augmented Chunking (SAC) as a mitigation technique — enriching each chunk with a document-level synthetic summary to inject global context lost during standard chunking. Experiments across a diverse set of legal information retrieval tasks show that SAC greatly reduces DRM and improves text-level retrieval precision and recall, with a generic summarization strategy found to outperform expert-guided summarization targeting specific legal elements (Reuter et al., 2024\) .

## **3.2 Methodology** {#3.2-methodology}

This study will follow an experimental research design by comparing five chunking strategies (fixed-size, recursive character, sentence-based, semantic, and section-aware) across three chunk sizes (256, 512, 1024 tokens). Three independent variables will be  systematically tested:

* Variable 1: Chunking Strategy  
* Variable 2: Chunk Size  
* Variable 3: Generator Model

All other pipeline components embedding model, retrieval depth (k=8), question template will be kept constant across all runs. This ensures that any difference in results can be attributed only to the variable being tested and nothing else.  
The experiment is structured in two phases:  
**Phase 1: Chunking Exploration**  
All 5 chunking strategies × 3 chunk sizes × 2 documents × 10 questions per document (20 questions in total) are tested using Llama-3.1-8B as the fixed generator model. This phase answers Objective 1, which chunking strategy and chunk size produce the best retrieval precision and answer quality on legal documents.  
**Phase 2: Model Comparison**  
The single best strategy and chunk size combination found in Phase 1 will be used with 2 generator models × 2 documents × 15 questions per document, giving all 30 question–answer pairs, which answers Objective 2\. All 30 pairs are used, rather than a subset, for two reasons. First, statistical power: with paired non-parametric tests, a sample of 10 questions can only detect very large differences between models, whereas n \= 30 allows moderate differences to reach significance. Second, validity: the 10 question–answer pairs not used during Phase 1 act as a held-out set, verifying that the configuration selected in Phase 1 was not tuned to the particular questions used to select it. Results will be reported for the full set and for the held-out subset separately.  
Each run will be evaluated on five metric groups: retrieval quality, faithfulness, correctness, latency, and token cost, as defined in Section 3.2.4. Results will be saved to PostgreSQL after every individual run so that no data is lost if the experiment is interrupted.

### **3.2.2 Data Collection Methods** {#3.2.2-data-collection-methods}

The project will use two Terms of Service documents, one from each of two different organisations operating in different industries. Picking from different industries to test how differently the same RAG setup works across very different document styles and content areas, rather than only within one type of business. Both documents will be public and downloaded from each organisation's website as PDFs. Each document will be around 10 to 30 pages long.  
For each document, 15 question-and-answer pairs will be written manually and verified against the source document giving 30 Q\&A pairs in total. The pairs cover a mix of question types so that the analysis can distinguish how different setups perform on different kinds of questions where each Q\&A record stores: the question, the expected answer, where in the document the answer comes from (which clause), the question type, and the document ID.

### **3.2.3 Ethical Considerations** {#3.2.3-ethical-considerations}

The project deals only with publicly available documents and does not involve any human subjects beyond researchers. As a result, no formal ethics committee approval is required. The following points are applied to ensure responsible research practice:

1. Public source documents only: Both Terms of Service documents will be  publicly published documents, on each organisation's website and freely accessible to anyone. The research will not be held on private contracts, internal policy documents, or any document that requires permission to view.  
2. No personally identifiable information: Terms of Service documents address users generically ("the User", "you", "the Customer") and do not contain personal information about specific individuals. So, no anonymisation step will be needed.  
3. No human participants: The 30 ground truth questions will be written by the researchers, not collected from external users. No surveys, interviews, or user studies will be conducted.  
4. Attribution and fair use: The two source documents will be clearly attributed to their respective organisations in the report. Only short excerpts will be quoted where needed to illustrate experimental results, in line with academic fair-use conventions.  
5. Open methodology and reproducibility: The pipeline code, prompts, ground truth questions, and aggregated results will be made available so that the study can be reproduced or extended. This supports research integrity and reduces the risk of misrepresentation.

### **3.2.4 Validation Techniques**  {#3.2.4-validation-techniques}

Validation will be applied at two levels: confirming the system works correctly before experiments begin, and confirming the metrics measure what they are supposed to measure.

- **Ground Truth Validation**  
  All 30 question-answer pairs (15 per TOS document) will be validated manually before any experiment runs. Each expected answer will be checked against the exact clause in the corresponding source document by both team members. Any disagreement will be resolved by re-reading the source document. This will ensure that errors in results come from the RAG pipeline itself, not from incorrect expected answers. Agreement between the two annotators prior to adjudication will be reported using Cohen's kappa.  
- **Evaluation Metrics and Statistical Analysis**  
  Each experimental run will be evaluated with mathematically defined metrics in four groups: retrieval quality, faithfulness, correctness, and efficiency. Because every configuration answers the same questions, all comparisons between configurations are paired at the question level, and every metric is computed per question and then macro-averaged across questions, reported as the mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval.  
  **Retrieval quality.** Each ground-truth record stores the character span of the clause in the source document that contains the answer. Because chunk boundaries change with every chunking configuration, chunk relevance cannot be annotated once; it is instead derived from the character overlap between each retrieved chunk and the gold clause span, following the character-level evaluation used in legal retrieval benchmarks (Pipitone & Houir Alami, 2024; Reuter et al., 2025). For a question with gold clause span G and retrieved chunks c₁ … c₈ (retrieval depth k \= 8 held constant), three metrics are computed: Character Recall@8 \= (characters of G contained in the retrieved chunks) ÷ (total characters of G), which measures how much of the answer clause was found; Character Precision@8 \= (characters of G contained in the retrieved chunks) ÷ (total characters retrieved), which measures how much of the retrieved text was actually relevant; and Hit Rate@8 \= 1 if any retrieved chunk overlaps G, else 0\. These metrics are deterministic and comparable across chunking configurations, which makes them suitable for Objective 1\.

**Faithfulness.** Following the RAGAS definition (Es et al., 2023), each generated answer is decomposed into atomic claims by an LLM, and each claim is checked against the retrieved chunks: Faithfulness F \= (number of claims supported by the retrieved context) ÷ (total number of claims). The claim-level hallucination rate is 1 − F. This measures grounding in the retrieved document text, independently of whether the answer matches the expected answer.  
**Correctness.** The headline correctness measure follows the CRAG benchmark's scoring scheme (Yang et al., 2024\) using reference-guided LLM-as-judge grading (Zheng et al., 2023). Claude Sonnet 5 — a model distinct from both generators, avoiding self-preference bias (Zheng et al., 2023\) — grades each answer against the verified expected answer at temperature 0 with a written rubric, as Accurate (+1), Missing (0, the system declined to answer), or Incorrect (−1). From these labels: Accuracy \= fraction Accurate; Hallucination rate \= fraction Incorrect; Missing rate \= fraction Missing; and Truthfulness \= Accuracy − Hallucination rate, which penalises confident wrong answers more heavily than abstentions. Two deterministic lexical measures are reported alongside as supporting evidence: token-level F1 and Exact Match as defined by the SQuAD evaluation script (Rajpurkar et al., 2016), and embedding cosine similarity between the generated and expected answers. Because grading is reference-guided, judge reliability does not depend on the judge outperforming the generators: the judge compares each answer against the verified expected answer rather than answering the question itself (Zheng et al., 2023).  
For the deliberately unanswerable questions, the correct behaviour is abstention. Abstention recall (the fraction of unanswerable questions correctly refused) and abstention precision (the fraction of refusals that were warranted) will be reported with raw counts (Kirichenko et al., 2025).  
**Judge validation.** Both team members will independently label a sample of judged answers; inter-annotator agreement will be reported as Cohen's kappa, κ \= (pₒ − pₑ) ÷ (1 − pₑ) (Landis & Koch, 1977), targeting κ ≥ 0.61 (“substantial”), and the judge's agreement with the adjudicated human labels will be reported as percentage agreement and κ, following the validation protocol of Zheng et al. (2023).  
**Efficiency.** Latency will be recorded as wall-clock time in milliseconds, instrumented separately for the retrieval and generation stages, and reported as median, 95th percentile, and mean per configuration. Token cost will be measured as total input plus output tokens per run, converted to monetary cost using the provider's published per-token prices.

- **Statistical Analysis**

Because all 15 Phase 1 configurations are evaluated on the same 20 questions, comparisons between configurations are paired at the question level. Three statistical tools are used to show that observed differences are real rather than chance (Demšar, 2006; Dror et al., 2018):  
**1\. Confidence intervals:** every reported mean carries a 95% bootstrap confidence interval, obtained by resampling the questions with replacement 10,000 times (Efron & Tibshirani, 1993), so that no result is reported as a bare average.  
**2\. Configuration comparison (Objective 1):** the best-performing configuration is compared against each of the other 14 using exact Wilcoxon signed-rank tests — a paired test that does not assume normally distributed scores — with Holm–Bonferroni correction (Holm, 1979\) to control the error rate across the 14 comparisons. In addition, to isolate the effect of each factor separately, per-question scores are averaged by chunking strategy (across its three chunk sizes) and by chunk size (across the five strategies), and these grouped means are reported with the same bootstrap confidence intervals, so that the influence of chunking strategy and of chunk size on answer quality can each be read directly.  
**3\. Model comparison (Objective 2):** the two generator models are compared per metric with the same exact Wilcoxon signed-rank test over the 30 paired question scores, alongside per-question win counts (for example, “Claude Opus 4.8 produced the better answer on 24 of 30 questions”) for interpretability.  
The hypotheses and the correction procedure will be fixed before the analysis begins. Comparable published chunking studies report point estimates without significance testing; this protocol therefore meets a higher evidential standard than is typical for the area.  
For Objective 1, all metrics will be evaluated across 20 questions (10 from each TOS document) using Llama-3.1-8B as the generation model. For Objective 2, the same metrics will be evaluated across all 30 questions (15 from each TOS document) using both Claude Opus 4.8 and Llama-3.1-8B, allowing direct comparison between the two models. Claude Sonnet 5 acts as the evaluation judge in both phases.  
**Presentation of Results**  
For Objective 1, results will be presented in three forms. First, a main results table listing all 15 configurations against every metric, with each cell reported as the mean and its 95% confidence interval and the best value in each column highlighted in bold. Second, a 5×3 strategy-by-size heatmap of the headline Truthfulness score, so that the combined effect of the two factors can be seen at a glance. Third, bar charts with confidence-interval error bars for the per-strategy and per-size grouped means, showing the isolated effect of each factor.  
For Objective 2, each metric will be summarised in a paired comparison table giving each model's mean with its 95% confidence interval, the difference between the models with its confidence interval, the Wilcoxon p-value, and the per-question win count. Latency will be visualised with box plots split by retrieval and generation stage, showing the median and 95th percentile, and token cost will be reported in a table converting token counts to monetary cost. All tables and figures will be generated programmatically from the PostgreSQL results tables, so every number in the report can be traced back to stored experimental runs and regenerated exactly.

- **Construct Validity**  
  All non-experimental variables, including the embedding model and retrieval depth (k=8), will be held constant across all runs. This will ensure that differences in scores are caused only by the variables being tested: chunking strategy and chunk size for Objective 1, and the choice of generation model for Objective 2\.

### **3.2.5 System Development method** {#3.2.5-system-development-method}

The iterative, module-based development approach will be chosen because it directly supports this requirement. Each module will be built and tested on its own with a fixed interface, so swapping any one module (a chunking strategy, an LLM backend) for the experiment is a single-file change that does not affect the rest of the pipeline.  
The seven modules:

1. Document Loader  
2. Chunker  
3. Embedder  
4. Vector Store  
5. Retriever  
6. Generator  
7. Evaluator

The development process will follow four sequential stages:

1. The first stage is building the modules. Each module will be developed independently and tested with hand-written examples. A module will be considered complete only when it passes all tests.   
2. The second stage is integrating the modules. Once every module has been individually tested, they will be connected into a single end-to-end pipeline. Three to five sample questions per TOS document will be run through the full pipeline to verify integration.   
3. The third stage is running the experiments. All experiments will be executed in two phases corresponding to the two objectives. Objective 1 will run 20 questions through Llama-3.1-8B across the chunking configurations, and Objective 2 will run all 30 questions through both Claude Opus 4.8 and Llama-3.1-8B, with Claude Sonnet 5 scoring every answer as the evaluation judge. After every run, results will be saved to PostgreSQL.  
4. The fourth stage is collecting and analysing findings. Results will be pulled from PostgreSQL, grouped by objective, and displayed on the dashboard, which renders the tables and figures defined in Section 3.2.4. The findings will then be written up, comparing chunking configurations for Objective 1 and generation models for Objective 2\.

# **CHAPTER 4** {#chapter-4}

# **RESEARCH PLAN AND BUDGET** {#research-plan-and-budget}

Two Terms of Service documents from two different organisations will be used as the source data. Fifteen question-answer pairs will be hand-written for each document, giving 30 pairs in total. Each expected answer will be verified against the exact clause in the source document before any testing begins. The questions for each document will be divided into four types. Four will be factual questions with answers found in a single clause, testing basic retrieval and extraction accuracy. Four will be multi-clause questions where the answer requires combining information from more than one clause. Four will be comparison questions that require finding and comparing two related clauses. There will be unanswerable questions where the answer does not exist in the document, testing whether the system correctly abstains rather than producing a hallucinated response.  
The following testing methods will be used throughout the project.

* **Unit Testing**  
  Each module of the pipeline will be tested individually before being connected to the rest of the system. A module will be considered ready only when all of its unit tests pass. This ensures that any errors found later during integration are caused by how the modules connect, not by faults within the modules themselves.

* **Integration Testing**  
  Once all modules pass their unit tests, they will be connected and tested as a complete pipeline. Integration testing will check that modules communicate correctly with each other and that data flows without errors from document ingestion through to answer generation.

* **Automated Testing**  
  Automated testing will be used during the main experiment to manage the large number of runs without manual monitoring. An experiment orchestrator will automatically loop through all configurations and trigger each run without manual intervention. For Objective 1, this covers five chunking strategies, three chunk sizes, two documents, and the relevant questions per document using Llama-3.1-8B. For Objective 2, this covers the best-performing configuration from Objective 1 tested across two generation models, two documents, and fifteen questions per document.  
  After each question is answered, the result will be automatically saved to PostgreSQL so that no data is lost if the experiment is interrupted. The orchestrator will check which question IDs have already been saved in the database and skip those, meaning only missing runs need to be re-executed. All metrics will be automatically calculated and saved after every run by the evaluator module.  
* **Manual Testing**  
  Manual testing will be carried out at two points: before the experiment to validate the system, and after the experiment to verify the results.  
- Before the experiment begins, both team members will verify each question-answer pair against the source document clause, and any disagreement will be corrected. A small set of three to five questions will then be run manually through the full pipeline to confirm the system is working correctly before automated runs begin. The demo chat interface will also be tested by typing questions and checking that answers and retrieved chunks display correctly.  
- After the experiment, a sample of generated answers from each configuration will be reviewed manually to confirm that metric scores align with human judgement. Any configuration that produces clearly incorrect answers but receives unexpectedly high scores will be flagged and inspected for evaluator bugs. The final results table will be checked to confirm there are no missing runs, duplicate rows, or incorrect metric values before analysis begins.

## **4.3 Budget** {#4.3-budget}

-  **Personnel Costs**

Personnel cost is the primary expense of this project, covering the development effort contributed by both team members across all project stages at a standard junior developer rate of NPR 300 per hour.

* Requirement Analysis and Planning: Both developers spend 30 hours each (60 hours total) on literature review, experiment design, and Q\&A pair creation, costs NPR 18,000   
* Module Development and Unit Testing: Both developers spend 50 hours each (100 hours total) building and testing all 7 pipeline modules, costs  NPR 30,000  
* Integration and Pipeline Setup: Both developers spend 20 hours each (40 hours total) connecting modules and running end-to-end tests, costs NPR 12,000  
* Experiment Execution and Monitoring: Both developers spend 15 hours each (30 hours total) running experiments and monitoring results, costs NPR 9,000  
* Frontend and Dashboard Development: Both developers spend 25 hours each (50 hours total) building the React UI and demo chat interface, costs NPR 15,000  
* Result Analysis and Visualisation: Both developers spend 20 hours each (40 hours total) querying results, generating charts, and interpreting findings, costs NPR 12,000  
* Total Developer Cost: NPR 96,000 (320 hours total across both developers)  
* Project Manager: Both team members share project management responsibilities jointly. No separate project manager is hired, NPR 0  
* QA Tester: Testing is carried out by both team members themselves as part of the development process. No separate QA tester is required, NPR 0  
* UI/UX Designer: The frontend is built using React with a simple functional interface. No dedicated UI/UX designer is needed, NPR 0  
- Development Tools and Software

All development tools used in this project fall within free tiers, resulting in zero software licensing or subscription costs.

* Cursor IDE \- Free  
* GitHub \- Free for student repositories  
* Cloudflare Workers and Workers AI \- Free tier sufficient for project scale  
* PostgreSQL via Supabase \- Free tier sufficient for storing all experiment results  
- **Infrastructure Costs**

The majority of infrastructure costs will be covered by Cloudflare's free tier. The only paid infrastructure item is the LLM API used in Phase 2\.

* Embedding Model (embeddinggemma-300m): Free via Cloudflare Workers AI  
* Paid LLM API (Claude Opus 4.8 for generation; Claude Sonnet 5 as the evaluation judge): NPR 2,500 – 4,000, estimated from the paid generation runs and approximately 1,500 short LLM-as-judge evaluation calls at published per-token prices. This is the only direct infrastructure cost in the entire project.

Total Cost Estimate

* Personnel / Developer Cost \= NPR 96,000  
* Infrastructure (Paid LLM API) \=  NPR 2,500 – 4,000  
* Additional Costs \=  NPR 4,000 – 4,500  
* Total Estimated Project Cost \= NPR 1,02,500 – 1,04,500

# **EXPECTED OUTCOME** {#expected-outcome}

## **5.1 Impact and Significance** {#5.1-impact-and-significance}

The project will produce two deliverables: 

- empirical findings from the experiment  
- a working application that demonstrates and explores those findings.

Both will contribute to the broader RAG community in different ways.  
The findings will have impact in three directions:

1. For developers building RAG systems for Terms of Service or similar legal document QA. The study will deliver a direct comparison table covering faithfulness, correctness, latency, and token cost across configurations on real ToS documents. Practitioners can read the recommended chunking strategy, chunk size, and generator model for their use case rather than running their own experiments or building systems with intuition based configurations.  
2. For RAG evaluation methodology. The implementation is released as part of the project and can be reused on other document corpora without depending on evaluation tools.  
3. For follow-up research. Because the three variables in this study will be tested while other configuration choices (embedding model, retrieval depth, prompt template, hybrid retrieval) will be held constant, the analysis provides a clean baseline that future studies can extend. The modular pipeline architecture allows any individual component to be swapped without rebuilding the rest.

The Demo UI, built on top of the best configuration, also has direct value as a usable consumer tool: a member of the public can ask a plain-language question about a Terms of Service document and receive an answer, demonstrating that the findings will be not theoretical but immediately applicable.
